name: Pitjantjatjara
catalog_quote: analyses presented in Tabain, Fletcher & Butcher (2014) show that the first syllable of the Pitjantjatjara word is marked by a raising of pitch and by extra duration, but that there is no evidence for secondary stress elsewhere in the word.
sweep_summary: Two sweep items. (1) Tabain, Fletcher & Butcher 2014 'Lexical stress in Pitjantjatjara' (J. Phonetics 42:52-66, doi 10.1016/j.wocn.2013.11.005): the primary instrumental study, directly about word stress in this language, but closed access everywhere checked (Unpaywall closed; OpenAlex closed, no repository fulltext; Semantic Scholar CLOSED with abstract elided; ScienceDirect 403; no Wayback snapshot); Harvard HOLLIS online access exists. Priority high. Its conclusion is already known second-hand from the authors' held JIPA Illustration (2014:198, the catalog's deciding quote, verified verbatim): initial syllable marked by raised pitch and extra duration, no evidence of secondary stress. (2) Glottolog's 'Rose 2005, Negotiating kinship: interpersonal prosodies in Pitjantjatjara (Word, 22pp)' resolves via Crossref to Rose 2008, WORD 59(1-2):189-215 (doi 10.1080/00437956.2008.11432586); its abstract, recovered from a Wayback snapshot of the paywalled T&F page and saved, shows a systemic-functional study of MOOD, MODAL ASSESSMENT and kinship exchanges -- 'prosody' in the SFL sense, silent on word stress; priority none. Re-read held/on-disk sources for the record: Rose 2001:112 and Langlois 2004:30-31 (first-hand: primary stress on the first syllable; Langlois adds secondary stress on di-/polymoraic suffix-initial vowels), Wilmoth & Mansfield 2021:11-12 (confirms) and Wilmoth 2023:88-89 (refines: Tabain et al. labelled strict SWSW alternation, so secondary stress on disyllabic suffixes remains open). Verdict: the catalog's fixed-initial coding and deciding source stand; no new source supersedes it.

new_statements.quote: Pitjantjatjara does not differ from this description and the initial vowel has primary stress. In the case of verbs prefixed by a directional prefix, both the prefix and first syllable of the verb have primary stress. [maa-pitja 'AWAY-go', ngalya-pitja 'THIS.WAY-go'] In case of dimoric and polymoric suffixes, the initial vowel of the suffix receives a secondary stress. [wangka-nytji-kitja 'talk-NOML-INTENT']
new_statements.citation: Langlois, Annie. 2004. Alive and Kicking: Areyonga Teenage Pitjantjatjara. Pacific Linguistics 561. Canberra: ANU. §2.3.2 'Stress', pp. 30-31.
new_statements.reading: Primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of the word (each directional prefix and its verb stem count as separate stress domains); the descriptive tradition adds secondary stress on the initial vowel of di-/polymoraic suffixes and on odd non-final syllables. This is the clearest first-hand descriptive statement read in this sweep, but it belongs to the impressionistic tradition whose alternating secondary stresses the instrumental study (Tabain, Fletcher & Butcher 2014, restated in the held JIPA 2014 p.198) failed to confirm. Nothing read here moves the catalog's fixed-initial coding; the only live nuance remains whether disyllabic suffixes carry secondary stress (Wilmoth 2023:88-89 keeps it open). Neither of the two sweep items yields a new first-hand statement: the J. Phonetics article is closed-access, and Rose 2005/2008 is SFL mood/modality, silent on word stress.

sources.citation: Langlois, Annie. 2004. Alive and Kicking: Areyonga Teenage Pitjantjatjara. Pacific Linguistics 561. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: Most commonly in Australian languages, primary stress (ˈ) goes onto the first syllable of the word. There is then often secondary stress (ˌ) on the third, fifth etc. syllables, excepting that the final syllable of a word does not usually bear stress (Dixon 1980:128). Pitjantjatjara does not differ from this description and the initial vowel has primary stress. In the case of verbs prefixed by a directional prefix, both the prefix and first syllable of the verb have primary stress. [...] In case of dimoric and polymoric suffixes, the initial vowel of the suffix receives a secondary stress.
sources.note: First-hand descriptive statement: primary stress on the initial vowel; both a directional prefix and the verb's first syllable carry primary stress; secondary stress on the initial vowel of dimoric/polymoric suffixes (and, following Dixon, on 3rd/5th syllables, never final). Confirms initial primary stress; posits the secondary stresses that the instrumental study did not find.

sources.citation: Rose, David. 2001. The Western Desert Code: An Australian Cryptogrammar. Pacific Linguistics 513. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: A foot begins with a stressed syllable, the Ictus, followed by a weak syllable, Remiss (see Abercrombie 1967). There is a very close complementarity in Western Desert between the foot and the word. Almost every word in the language is spoken with the stress on the first syllable, both in isolation, as in Figure 2.21, and in larger structures of group and clause.
sources.locator: §2.5.3 'Stress wave', p.112 (text lines 5934-5941); summary at ch.2 p.29 (line 1039)
sources.note: First-hand: almost every word is stressed on its first syllable; a foot = stressed Ictus + Remiss (+ one or two enclitic syllables); multisyllabic suffixes can be spoken on a dependent foot (p.29 summary). Confirms initial primary stress.

sources.citation: Wilmoth, Sasha. 2023 [submitted 2022]. The Dynamics of Contemporary Pitjantjatjara: An Intergenerational Study. PhD thesis, University of Melbourne. hdl.handle.net/11343/325722 (open access).
sources.quote: Summarises all prior descriptions (Douglas 1957; Marsh 1969; Glass & Hackett 1970; Goddard 1985; Hansen & Hansen 1969/1978; Langlois 2004; Rose 2001): 'Primary stress on the first syllable of the prosodic word ... Secondary stress on odd numbered syllables thereafter; Secondary stress on the first syllable of disyllabic suffixes; Final syllables do not bear stress.' Then: 'Tabain et al. (2014) found several phonetic correlates strongly associated with word-initial primary stress, but no evidence for secondary stress. However, their findings do not completely resolve the question ... Secondary
sources.note: Summarises the descriptive tradition (initial primary stress; secondary stress on odd syllables and on the first syllable of disyllabic suffixes; final syllables unstressed); accepts Tabain et al.'s finding of word-initial primary stress but argues their strictly alternating SWSW labelling did not test the disyllabic-suffix claim, so secondary stress in morphologically complex words 'remains unresolved'; independently analyses feet as bimoraic, left-to-right. Initial primary stress is secure; the catalog's 'strict' (no secondary) reading is what the instrumental evidence supports but Wilmoth…

sources.citation: Wilmoth, Sasha & John Mansfield. 2021. Inflectional predictability and prosodic morphology in Pitjantjatjara and Yankunytjatjara. Morphology 31:355-401 (doi 10.1007/s11525-021-09380-y); author preprint, 40 pp.
sources.quote: Same four-bullet summary of the traditional descriptions ('Primary stress on the first syllable of the word ... Secondary stress on odd numbered syllables thereafter ... Final syllables do not bear stress'), then 'A phonetic analysis of Pitjantjatjara by Tabain et al. (2014) has cast doubt on the existence of secondary stress, which is posited in most previous descriptions. However, there is evidence for metrical structure apart from the presence or absence of secondary stress.' Analyses feet as bimoraic, not disyllabic.
sources.note: Compact verbatim summary of every traditional stress description plus the bimoraic-foot analysis; useful as the citable statement of the older alternating-secondary-stress tradition our coding sets aside.

sources.quote: The goal of this paper is to give the the first reader sense of the rich varieties of discourse through which speakers of the Australian language Pitjantjatjara enact their social relations. The brief sketch here is based on a fuller survey in Rose 2001, using the tools of systemic functional linguistics (SFL) for relating language to its social contexts. The discussion involves three steps: firstly, an outline of the options for enacting interpersonal meanings in Pitjantjatjara, in its systems of MOOD and MODAL ASSESSMENT, secondly, an outline of the system of social relations in Pitjantjatjara culture, governed by the kinship system, and finally, examples of exchanges between various kin
sources.locator: abstract, WORD 59(1-2):189 (Wayback snapshot 2022-06-15 of the T&F abstract page)
sources.note: Abstract (from the archived Taylor & Francis page): the paper sketches, using systemic functional linguistics, 'the options for enacting interpersonal meanings in Pitjantjatjara, in its systems of MOOD and MODAL ASSESSMENT', the kinship system, and exchanges between kin. 'Interpersonal prosodies' is the SFL term (Rose 2001 §2.4.1, p.99-100: 'prosodies of sounding and wording... The phonological prosody is carried on a tonicity wave that rises and falls in pitch'), i.e. mood/modality and intonation spread over the clause, not word-stress placement.
